Beginning with the battle of Borodino, from which point his disagreement with those around him began, he alone said that Borodino was a victory, and he repeated this both verbally and in his dispatches and reports until his death. He alone said that the loss of Moscow did not mean the loss of Russia. In reply to Lauriston's proposal of peace, he said: There can be no peace, for such is the people's will. He alone, during the French retreat, said that all their maneuvers were useless, that everything was working out better than they could wish without them, that the enemy must be offered a "golden bridge," that the battles at Tarutino, Vyazma, and Krasnoe were unnecessary, that they needed to keep enough strength to reach the border, and that he would not sacrifice a single Russian for ten Frenchmen.

And this courtier, as he is portrayed—who lies to Arakcheev to please the Emperor—he alone, at the cost of the Emperor's displeasure, said in Vilna that to carry the war beyond the frontier was useless and harmful.

Nor do his words alone prove that he understood the meaning of events. His actions—without the slightest deviation—were all directed toward one and the same threefold end: (1) to concentrate all his strength for the conflict with the French, (2) to defeat them, and (3) to drive them out of Russia, while minimizing as far as possible the suffering of his people and his army.

This supposed procrastinator Kutuzov, whose motto was "Patience and Time," this supposed enemy of decisive action, gave battle at Borodino and invested the preparations for it with unparalleled solemnity. This Kutuzov, who before the battle of Austerlitz said it would be lost, he alone, contradicting everyone else, declared to his dying day that Borodino was a victory—despite the assurance of generals that the battle was lost and the unprecedented fact that an army had to retreat after winning. He alone, throughout the entire retreat, insisted that further battles were useless, that a new war should not be begun, and that the Russian frontier should not be crossed.

It is easy now to understand the significance of these events—if only we refrain from attributing to the actions of the masses aims that existed only in the heads of a dozen people—for the events and their results now lie before us.
But how did that old man, alone, in opposition to the general opinion, so accurately perceive the importance of the people's view of events that in all his actions he was never once untrue to it?
The source of that extraordinary power of insight lay in the national feeling that he possessed in full purity and strength.

Only the recognition that he possessed this feeling caused the people, in such a strange manner and contrary to the Tsar's wish, to choose him—an old man in disfavor—as their representative in the national war. And only that feeling placed him on the highest pedestal from which he, the commander in chief, devoted all his powers not to slaying and destroying men but to saving them and showing them pity.
That simple, modest, and therefore truly great figure could not be forced into the false mold of a European hero—the supposed ruler of men—that history has fabricated.
To a servant, no man can be great, because a servant has his own idea of what greatness means.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: November fifth was the first day of what is called the battle of Krasnoe. Toward evening—after much arguing and many mistakes by generals who went to the wrong places, after adjutants had been sent racing about with counter-orders—when it became clear that the enemy was in full flight everywhere and that there could be no battle, Kutuzov left Krasnoe and went to Dobroe, where his headquarters had been transferred that day.

The day was clear and frosty. Kutuzov rode to Dobroe on his plump little white horse, followed by an enormous retinue of discontented generals who whispered among themselves behind his back. All along the road, groups of French prisoners captured that day—there were seven thousand of them—crowded around campfires to warm themselves. Near Dobroe, an immense crowd of tattered prisoners, buzzing with talk and wrapped and bandaged in whatever they could find, stood in the road beside a long row of unharnessed French guns. At the approach of the commander in chief, the buzz of talk ceased and all eyes turned to Kutuzov, who wore a white cap with a red band and a padded overcoat that bulged on his round shoulders as he moved slowly along the road on his white horse. One of the generals was reporting where the guns and prisoners had been captured.

Kutuzov seemed distracted and wasn't listening. He squinted with a dissatisfied expression as he studied the prisoners, who presented an especially wretched sight. Most of them were disfigured by frostbitten noses and cheeks, and nearly all had red, swollen, and festering eyes.

One group of Frenchmen stood close to the road, and two of them—one with his face covered in sores—were tearing at a piece of raw flesh with their hands. There was something horrible and animal-like in the fleeting glance they cast at the riders and in the hostile expression with which the soldier with the sores immediately turned away and went back to what he was doing.

Kutuzov looked long and hard at these two soldiers. He puckered his face, squinted, and pensively nodded his head. At another spot, he noticed a Russian soldier laughingly patting a Frenchman on the shoulder and saying something to him in a friendly way, and Kutuzov nodded his head again with the same expression.

"What were you saying?" he asked the general, who was continuing his report and directing the commander in chief's attention to some captured French standards standing before the Preobrazhensky regiment.
"Ah, the standards!" said Kutuzov, clearly pulling himself back with difficulty from the thoughts that preoccupied him.
He looked around absently. Thousands of eyes were watching him from all sides, waiting for a word from him.

He stopped in front of the Preobrazhensky regiment, sighed deeply, and closed his eyes. Someone on his staff beckoned to the soldiers carrying the standards to come forward and surround the commander in chief. Kutuzov was silent for several seconds, then, submitting with obvious reluctance to the duty imposed by his position, raised his head and began to speak. A crowd of officers gathered around him. He looked carefully at the circle of officers, recognizing several of them.

"I thank you all!" he said, addressing the soldiers and then the officers again. In the stillness around him, his slowly spoken words were clearly audible. "I thank you all for your hard and faithful service. The victory is complete, and Russia will not forget you! Honor to you forever."
He paused and looked around.

"Lower its head, lower it!" he said to a soldier who had accidentally lowered the French eagle he was holding in front of the Preobrazhensky standards. "Lower, lower, that's it. Hurrah, lads!" he added, with a quick motion of his chin.
"Hur-r-rah!" roared thousands of voices.
While the soldiers were shouting, Kutuzov leaned forward in his saddle and bowed his head, and his eye lit up with a mild and seemingly ironic gleam.

"You see, brothers..." he said when the shouts had died away... and all at once his voice and the expression on his face changed. It was no longer the commander in chief speaking but an ordinary old man who wanted to tell his comrades something very important.
A stir ran through the crowd of officers and the soldiers' ranks as they pressed forward to hear better what he was going to say.

"You see, brothers, I know it's hard for you, but it can't be helped! Bear up—it won't be long now! We'll see our visitors off and then we'll rest. The Tsar won't forget your service. It's hard for you, but still you're at home, while they—you see what they've come to," he said, pointing at the prisoners. "Worse off than our poorest beggars. While they were strong, we didn't spare ourselves, but now we can even pity them. They're human beings too. Isn't that right, lads?"

He looked around, and in the direct, respectful, wondering gazes fixed on him, he read agreement with what he had said. His face grew brighter and brighter with an old man's gentle smile, drawing the corners of his lips and eyes into a web of wrinkles. He stopped speaking and bowed his head as if in thought.
"But then again, who asked them to come here? Serves them right, the bloody bastards!" he suddenly cried, raising his head.
And flourishing his whip, he rode off at a gallop for the first time during the entire campaign, leaving behind the broken ranks of soldiers who were laughing joyfully and shouting "Hurrah!"

Kutuzov's actual words were barely understood by the troops. No one could have repeated the field marshal's speech, which began solemnly and ended as an old man's simple, heartfelt talk. But the genuine sincerity of that speech, the feeling of triumphant majesty combined with pity for the enemy and an awareness of the justice of their cause—expressed so perfectly by that old man's good-natured final outburst—was not merely understood but lived in the soul of every soldier and found expression in their joyous, prolonged cheering. Afterward, when one of the generals asked Kutuzov whether he wanted his carriage sent for, Kutuzov unexpectedly gave a sob in his reply, clearly deeply moved.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: When the troops reached their night's stopping place on November eighth—the last day of the Krasnoe battles—it was already growing dark. All day it had been calm and frosty with occasional light snow, and toward evening the sky began to clear. Through the falling snow, a purple-black starry sky appeared and the frost grew sharper.

An infantry regiment that had left Tarutino three thousand strong but now numbered only nine hundred was one of the first to arrive at the halting place—a village on the highway. The quartermasters who met the regiment reported that all the huts were full of sick and dead Frenchmen, cavalrymen, and members of the staff. Only one hut was available for the regimental commander.
The commander rode up to his hut. The regiment passed through the village and stacked its arms in front of the last houses.

Like some huge, many-limbed animal, the regiment began to prepare its shelter and food. One part dispersed and waded knee-deep through snow into a birch forest to the right of the village, and immediately the sounds of axes, swords crashing through branches, and merry voices could be heard from there. Another group busied itself around the regimental wagons and horses, getting out kettles and hardtack and feeding the horses. A third section scattered through the village, arranging quarters for the staff officers, hauling out French corpses from the huts, and dragging away boards, dry wood, and thatch from the roofs for campfires, or fence panels for shelter.
About fifteen men with merry shouts were shaking down the tall wattle wall of a shed whose roof had already been removed.

"Now then, all together—push!" cried the voices, and the huge surface of the wall, sprinkled with snow and creaking with frost, swayed in the darkness of the night. The lower stakes cracked more and more, and finally the wall fell, along with the men who had been pushing it. Loud, rough laughter and joyous shouts followed.
"Now then, grab it in pairs! Hand up the lever! That's it... Where are you shoving?"
"Now, all together! But wait a moment, boys... With a song!"

Everyone fell silent, and a soft, pleasant, velvety voice began to sing. At the end of the third verse, as the last note died away, twenty voices roared out at once: "Oo-oo-oo-oo! That's it. All together! Heave away, boys!" But despite their combined efforts, the wattle hardly moved, and in the silence that followed, the heavy breathing of the men was the only sound.
"Hey, Sixth Company! You devils! Give us a hand... We might need you one of these days."

About twenty men from the Sixth Company, who were on their way into the village, joined the haulers, and the wattle wall—about thirty-five feet long and seven feet high—moved forward along the village street, swaying, pressing on and cutting into the shoulders of the gasping men.
"Get along... Falling? What are you stopping for? There now..."
Cheerful, meaningless abuse flowed freely.

"What do you think you're doing?" came the sharp, authoritative voice of a sergeant major who came upon the men hauling their load. "There are officers here! The general himself is in that hut, and you foul-mouthed brutes! I'll give it to you!" he shouted, hitting the first man he reached a swinging blow on the back. "Can't you keep it down?"
The men fell silent. The soldier who had been struck groaned and wiped his face, which had been scratched bloody when he fell against the wattle.
"There, see how that devil hits! He's made my face all bloody," he said in a frightened whisper when the sergeant major had passed.
"Don't you like it?" said a laughing voice, and lowering their tones, the men moved on.
Once they were out of the village, they began talking again just as loudly as before, larding their conversation with the same pointless profanity.

In the hut the men had passed, the senior officers had gathered and were in animated discussion over tea about the day's events and the maneuvers proposed for the next day. The plan was to make a flanking march to the left, cut off the Viceroy (Murat), and capture him.

By the time the soldiers had dragged the wattle fence into place, campfires were blazing on all sides. Wood crackled, snow melted, and black shadows of soldiers moved back and forth across the trampled area.

Axes and hatchets rang out everywhere. Everything was done without any orders being given. Firewood was gathered for the night, shelters were put up for the officers, kettles were boiling, and muskets and equipment were put in order.

The wattle wall the men had brought was set up in a semicircle by the Eighth Company as a windbreak against the north, propped up by musket rests, with a campfire built in front of it. They beat the evening drum, called the roll, had supper, and settled around the fires for the night—some mending their footwear, some smoking pipes, and some stripping naked to steam the lice out of their shirts.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The Fifth Company was camped at the very edge of the forest. A huge campfire blazed brightly in the middle of the snow, lighting up the branches of trees heavy with frost.
Around midnight they heard footsteps in the snow and the cracking of dry branches in the forest.
"A bear, lads," said one of the men.
They all raised their heads to listen, and out of the forest into the bright firelight stepped two strangely dressed human figures clinging to each other.

They were two Frenchmen who had been hiding in the forest. They came up to the fire, hoarsely saying something in a language the Russian soldiers didn't understand. One was taller than the other; he wore an officer's hat and seemed completely exhausted. As he approached the fire and tried to sit down, he fell. The other, a short, sturdy soldier with a shawl tied around his head, was stronger. He lifted his companion and said something, pointing to his mouth. The Russian soldiers gathered around the Frenchmen, spread a greatcoat on the ground for the sick man, and brought buckwheat porridge and vodka for both of them.
The exhausted French officer was Ramballe, and the man with the shawl around his head was Morel, his orderly.

When Morel had drunk some vodka and finished his bowl of porridge, he suddenly became unnaturally cheerful and chattered nonstop to the soldiers, who couldn't understand him. Ramballe refused food and, resting his head on his elbow, lay silent beside the campfire, staring at the Russian soldiers with red, vacant eyes. Occasionally he let out a long groan, then fell silent again. Morel, pointing to his shoulders, tried to convey that Ramballe was an officer and ought to be warmed. A Russian officer who had approached the fire sent to ask his colonel whether he would take a French officer into his hut, and when the messenger returned saying the colonel agreed, Ramballe was told to go. He rose and tried to walk but staggered and would have fallen if a nearby soldier hadn't caught him.
"You won't try that again, eh?" said one of the soldiers, winking and turning mockingly to Ramballe.
"Oh, you fool! Why talk rubbish, you oaf—a real peasant!" came rebukes from every side at the joking soldier.
They surrounded Ramballe, lifted him onto the crossed arms of two soldiers, and carried him to the hut. Ramballe put his arms around their necks as they carried him and began wailing plaintively:
"Oh, you fine fellows, my kind, kind friends! These are real men! Oh, my brave, kind friends!" And he rested his head on one soldier's shoulder like a child.
Meanwhile, Morel was sitting in the best spot by the fire, surrounded by soldiers.

Morel, a short, sturdy Frenchman with inflamed, streaming eyes, wore a woman's cloak and had a shawl tied around his head over his cap, babushka-style. He was clearly tipsy and was singing a French song in a hoarse, broken voice with one arm thrown around the nearest soldier. The soldiers simply held their sides watching him.
"Come on, come on, teach us how it goes! I'll pick it up quick. How does it go?" said a man who was both a singer and a comedian, the one Morel was embracing.
"Long live Henry the Fourth! Long live that brave king!" sang Morel, winking. "That rowdy devil..."
("Long live Henry the Fourth, that valiant king! That rowdy devil.")
"Vivarika! Vif-seruvaru! Sedyablyaka!" the soldier repeated, waving his arm and actually catching the tune.
"Bravo! Ha, ha, ha!" Rough, joyful laughter burst from all sides.
Morel, wrinkling up his face, laughed too.
"Well, go on, go on!"
"Who had a triple talent—for drinking, for fighting, and for being a charming fellow..."
(Who had a triple talent—for drinking, for fighting, and for being a gallant old boy...)
"Smooth, that is. Come on now, Zaletaev!"
"Ke..." Zaletaev brought out with effort: "ke-e-e-e," he drawled, laboriously pursing his lips, "le-trip-ta-la-de-bu-de-ba, e de-tra-va-ga-la," he sang.
"Fine! Just like the Frenchman! Ho ho ho! Want some more to eat?"
"Give him some porridge—it takes a long time to fill up after you've been starving."

They gave him more porridge and Morel, laughing, set to work on his third bowl. All the young soldiers watched him with beaming smiles. The older men, who considered it beneath their dignity to amuse themselves with such nonsense, continued lying on the other side of the fire, but one would occasionally prop himself up on an elbow and glance at Morel with a smile.
"They're human beings too," said one of them as he wrapped himself in his coat. "Even weeds grow from their own roots."
"Oh Lord, oh Lord! How starry it is! Incredible! That means a hard frost..."

They all fell quiet. The stars, as if knowing that no one was watching them, began to play in the dark sky: now flaring up, now vanishing, now trembling, they whispered among themselves something joyful and mysterious.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: The French army melted away at the steady rate of a mathematical progression, and the crossing of the Berezina—about which so much has been written—was only one intermediate stage in its destruction, not at all the decisive episode of the campaign. If so much has been and still is written about the Berezina, on the French side this is only because at the broken bridge across that river, the calamities the army had been enduring were suddenly concentrated into a single tragic spectacle that seared itself into every memory. On the Russian side, it's simply because in Petersburg—far from the actual fighting—yet another plan (one of Pfuel's) had been devised to trap Napoleon at the Berezina River. Everyone was certain that everything would go according to plan, and therefore insisted that it was the Berezina crossing that destroyed the French army. In reality, the results of the crossing were far less disastrous to the French—in guns and men lost—than Krasnoe had been, as the numbers show.

The sole importance of the Berezina crossing lies in the fact that it plainly and undeniably proved the bankruptcy of all the plans to cut off the enemy's retreat, and confirmed the soundness of the only possible course of action—the one Kutuzov and the mass of the army demanded—which was simply to follow the enemy. The French mob fled at ever-increasing speed, all its energy directed toward reaching its goal. It fled like a wounded animal, and it was impossible to block its path. This was shown not so much by its arrangements for crossing as by what happened at the bridges. When the bridges collapsed, unarmed soldiers, civilians from Moscow, and women with children who were traveling with the French—all carried forward by sheer momentum—piled into boats and onto the ice-covered water and refused to surrender.

That impulse was entirely rational. The condition of both fugitives and pursuers was equally miserable. As long as they stayed with their own people, each could hope for help from comrades and hold a defined place among them. But those who surrendered, while remaining in the same wretched state, would drop to a lower level in any claim on the necessities of life. The French didn't need to be told that half the prisoners—whom the Russians didn't know what to do with—perished of cold and hunger despite their captors' desire to save them. They sensed it could not be otherwise. The most compassionate Russian commanders, those favorably disposed toward the French—even Frenchmen serving in the Russian army—could do nothing for the prisoners. The French perished from the very conditions to which the Russian army itself was exposed. It was impossible to take bread and clothing from starving, essential Russian soldiers to give to Frenchmen who, though not threatening or hated or guilty, were simply unnecessary. Some Russians even did that, but they were exceptions.

Certain destruction lay behind the French, but ahead lay hope. Their bridges had been burned; there was no salvation except in collective flight, and on that the whole strength of the French was concentrated.

The farther they fled, the more wretched became the plight of the remnant—especially after the Berezina, on which (thanks to the Petersburg plan) the Russians had placed such high hopes—and the more heated grew the passions of the Russian commanders, who blamed one another and above all Kutuzov. Anticipating that the failure of the Petersburg Berezina plan would be blamed on Kutuzov led to increasing dissatisfaction, contempt, and ridicule. The ridicule and contempt were expressed, of course, in respectful form, making it impossible for him to ask what exactly he was being accused of. They didn't talk seriously to him; when reporting or asking for his approval, they appeared to be fulfilling an unpleasant formality while winking behind his back and trying to undermine him at every turn.

Because they couldn't understand him, all these people assumed it was useless to talk to the old man; that he would never grasp the profundity of their plans; that he would answer with his stock phrases about a "golden bridge," the impossibility of crossing the frontier with a mob of ragged men, and so on. They had heard all that before. And everything he said—that they needed to wait for supplies, that the men had no boots—was so simple, while what they proposed was so complex and clever, that it was obvious he was a stupid old man while they, though not in command, were military geniuses.

After the junction with the army of the brilliant admiral and Petersburg hero Wittgenstein, this mood and staff gossip reached a peak. Kutuzov saw this and merely sighed and shrugged. Only once, after the affair at the Berezina, did he get angry and write the following letter to Bennigsen (who reported separately to the Emperor):

"On account of your frequent bouts of ill health, would Your Excellency kindly be so good as to proceed to Kaluga upon receipt of this, there to await further commands and appointments from His Imperial Majesty."

But after Bennigsen's departure, the Grand Duke Constantine Pavlovich joined the army. He had participated at the beginning of the campaign but had been removed by Kutuzov. Now, returning to the army, he informed Kutuzov of the Emperor's displeasure at the slow progress and poor results. The Emperor intended to join the army personally in a few days.

The old man, experienced in both court and military affairs—this same Kutuzov who in August had been chosen commander in chief against the sovereign's wishes, who had removed the Grand Duke and heir apparent from the army, who on his own authority and contrary to the Emperor's will had decided to abandon Moscow—now instantly understood that his day was over, his role played out, and the power he supposedly held was no longer his. And he understood this not merely from the court's attitude. He saw, on the one hand, that the military campaign in which he had played his part was finished, and he felt his mission was accomplished. At the same time, he began to feel the physical weariness of his aged body and the need for rest.

On November twenty-ninth, Kutuzov entered Vilna—his "dear Vilna," as he called it. Twice during his career he had been governor of Vilna. In that wealthy city, which had not been damaged, he found old friends and associations as well as the comforts of life he had so long been deprived of. And he suddenly turned from the cares of army and state, and as far as the passions seething around him allowed, immersed himself in the quiet life he had once known, as if everything happening in the world of history no longer concerned him at all.

Chichagov—one of the most zealous proponents of "cutting off" and "breaking through," who had first wanted to operate in Greece, then in Warsaw, but never wished to go where he was actually sent; Chichagov, noted for his bold manner of speaking to the Emperor, and who considered Kutuzov indebted to him (because when he was sent to conclude peace with Turkey in 1811, independently of Kutuzov, he found the peace already made and acknowledged to the Emperor that the credit belonged to Kutuzov)—this Chichagov was the first to meet Kutuzov at the castle where the latter was to stay. In undress naval uniform, carrying a dirk with his cap under his arm, he handed Kutuzov a garrison report and the keys to the city. The contemptuous-yet-respectful attitude of the younger generation toward the old man in his dotage was expressed to the highest degree in Chichagov's behavior, as he was well aware of the accusations being leveled at Kutuzov.
In conversation with Chichagov, Kutuzov happened to mention that the vehicles packed with china captured from him at Borisov had been recovered and would be returned.

"You mean to imply that I have nothing to eat from? On the contrary, I can supply you with everything, even if you want to throw dinner parties," Chichagov replied warmly, trying with every word to prove his own integrity and therefore imagining Kutuzov was driven by the same concern.
Kutuzov, shrugging his shoulders, replied with his subtle, knowing smile: "I merely meant what I said."

Contrary to the Emperor's wishes, Kutuzov kept the greater part of the army in Vilna. Those around him said he became extraordinarily slack and physically feeble during his stay. He attended to army business reluctantly, left everything to his generals, and while waiting for the Emperor to arrive led a leisurely life.

The Emperor left Petersburg on December seventh with his retinue—Count Tolstoy, Prince Volkonsky, Arakcheev, and others—and reached Vilna on the eleventh. In his traveling sleigh, he drove straight to the castle. Despite the severe frost, about a hundred generals and staff officers in full dress uniform stood before the castle, along with a guard of honor from the Semenov regiment.
A courier galloping ahead in a troika with three foam-flecked horses shouted "Coming!" and Konovnitsyn rushed into the vestibule to inform Kutuzov, who was waiting in the porter's lodge.

A minute later, the old man's large, heavy figure in full-dress uniform—his chest covered with medals and a sash wrapped around his stomach—waddled out onto the porch. He put on his two-pointed hat, and holding his gloves in one hand, walked with effort sideways down the steps to street level, taking in his other hand the report he had prepared for the Emperor.

There was running to and fro and whispering; another troika flew up at great speed, and then all eyes turned to an approaching sleigh in which the figures of the Emperor and Volkonsky could already be seen.

From the force of fifty years' habit, all this had a physically exciting effect on the old general. He carefully felt himself all over, adjusted his hat, and pulling himself together, drew himself upright. At the very moment the Emperor stepped down from the sleigh and looked up at him, Kutuzov handed over the report and began speaking in his smooth, ingratiating voice.

The Emperor swept a rapid glance over Kutuzov from head to foot, frowned for an instant, but immediately composed himself, stepped forward, extended his arms, and embraced the old man. This embrace too, because of a deep-seated emotional association, had its usual effect on Kutuzov, and he gave a sob.
The Emperor greeted the officers and the Semenov guard, then pressed the old man's hand again and went into the castle with him.

When alone with the field marshal, the Emperor expressed his dissatisfaction at the slowness of the pursuit and the mistakes made at Krasnoe and the Berezina, and outlined his plans for a future campaign abroad. Kutuzov made no objection or comment. The same submissive, expressionless look with which he had listened to the Emperor's orders on the field of Austerlitz seven years before settled on his face.
When Kutuzov came out of the study and was crossing the ballroom with his heavy, waddling gait, head bowed, someone's voice stopped him:
"Your Serene Highness!"

Kutuzov raised his head and looked for a long time into the eyes of Count Tolstoy, who stood before him holding a silver tray on which lay a small object. Kutuzov seemed not to understand what was expected of him.

Suddenly he appeared to remember. A barely perceptible smile flickered across his puffy face, and bowing low and respectfully, he took the object from the tray. It was the Order of St. George, First Class.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The next day the field marshal gave a dinner and ball that the Emperor honored with his presence. Kutuzov had received the Order of St. George, First Class, and the Emperor showed him the highest honors, but everyone knew of the imperial displeasure. The forms were observed and the Emperor was the first to set the example, yet everybody understood that the old man was considered at fault and good for nothing. When Kutuzov, following an old tradition from Catherine's day, ordered the captured standards lowered at the Emperor's feet as he entered the ballroom, the Emperor made a face and muttered something in which some people caught the words "the old comedian."
The Emperor's displeasure with Kutuzov was especially heightened at Vilna by the fact that Kutuzov clearly could not or would not understand the importance of the coming campaign.
When the Emperor told the assembled officers the following morning: "You have not only saved Russia, you have saved Europe!" they all understood that the war was not over.

Kutuzov alone refused to see this and openly stated that no new war could improve Russia's position or add to her glory, but could only diminish the glorious standing Russia had won. He tried to demonstrate to the Emperor the impossibility of raising fresh troops, spoke of the hardships the people had already endured, of the possibility of failure, and so on.
Given the field marshal's frame of mind, he was naturally regarded as nothing more than a hindrance and obstacle to the impending war.

To avoid unpleasant confrontations with the old man, the natural solution was to do what had been done with him at Austerlitz and with Barclay at the start of the Russian campaign: transfer authority to the Emperor himself, thus pulling the rug from under the commander in chief without upsetting the old man by telling him directly.

To this end, his staff was gradually restructured and its real power removed and transferred to the Emperor. Toll, Konovnitsyn, and Ermolov received new appointments. Everyone spoke openly of the field marshal's great weakness and failing health.
His health had to be bad for his position to be taken from him and given to another. And indeed his health was poor.

So naturally, simply, and gradually—just as he had come from Turkey to Petersburg to recruit the militia, and then to the army when he was needed—now that his part was played, Kutuzov's place was taken by a new and necessary performer.
The war of 1812, besides its national significance dear to every Russian heart, was now to take on another, European significance.

The movement of peoples from west to east was to be followed by a movement from east to west, and for this new war another leader was needed—one with different qualities and views, driven by different motives.
Alexander I was as necessary for the movement of peoples from east to west and for the redrawing of national boundaries as Kutuzov had been for the salvation and glory of Russia.

Kutuzov did not understand what Europe, the balance of power, or Napoleon meant. He could not understand it. For the representative of the Russian people, after the enemy had been destroyed and Russia had been liberated and raised to the summit of her glory, there was nothing left to do as a Russian. Nothing remained for the representative of the national war but to die. And Kutuzov died.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: As generally happens, Pierre did not feel the full effects of the physical privation and strain he had endured as a prisoner until after they were over. After his liberation, he reached Orel, and on the third day there, when preparing to continue to Kiev, he fell ill and was bedridden for three months. He had what the doctors called "bilious fever." But despite the fact that they treated him, bled him, and gave him medicine, he recovered.

Very little impression was left on Pierre's mind by everything that happened from his rescue to his illness. He remembered only the dull gray weather, now rainy and now snowy, internal physical distress, and pains in his feet and side. He recalled a general impression of people's misfortunes and suffering, of being pestered by the curiosity of officers and generals who questioned him, and the difficulty of finding a carriage and horses. Above all, he remembered his inability to think and feel during that time. On the day of his rescue, he had seen Petya Rostov's body. That same day, he learned that Prince Andrew, after surviving the battle of Borodino by more than a month, had recently died at the Rostovs' house in Yaroslavl, and Denisov, who told him this, also mentioned Helene's death, assuming Pierre had heard about it long ago. All of this seemed merely strange to Pierre at the time—he felt unable to grasp its significance. Just then, his only desire was to get away as quickly as possible from places where people were killing one another, to some peaceful refuge where he could recover, rest, and make sense of all the strange new things he had learned. But upon reaching Orel, he immediately fell ill. When he came to after his illness, he saw two of his servants attending him—Terenty and Vaska, who had come from Moscow—as well as his cousin the eldest princess, who had been living on his estate at Yelets and, hearing of his rescue and illness, had come to look after him.

It was only gradually during his recovery that Pierre shed the impressions he had grown accustomed to over the past months and got used to the idea that no one would force him to go anywhere tomorrow, that no one would take away his warm bed, and that he would certainly get his dinner, tea, and supper. But for a long time he still dreamed of captivity. In the same gradual way, he came to absorb the news he had been told after his rescue: the death of Prince Andrew, the death of his wife, and the destruction of the French.

A joyous feeling of freedom—that complete, innate freedom natural to every person, which he had first experienced at the initial halt outside Moscow—filled Pierre's soul during his recovery. He was surprised to find that this inner freedom, which was independent of external circumstances, now came with the added bonus of external liberty. He was alone in a strange town, without acquaintances. No one demanded anything of him or sent him anywhere. He had everything he wanted; the thought of his wife, which had been a constant torment, was gone now that she was no more.

"Oh, how wonderful! How splendid!" he said to himself when a neatly set table was brought to him with savory broth, or when he lay down at night in a soft, clean bed, or when he remembered that the French were gone and his wife was no more. "Oh, how wonderful, how splendid!"
And from old habit he asked himself: "Well, and what next? What am I going to do?" And he immediately gave himself the answer: "Well, I shall live. Ah, how splendid!"

The very question that had formerly tormented him, the thing he had endlessly sought—the aim of life—no longer existed for him now. That search for an aim hadn't merely disappeared temporarily; he felt it no longer existed and could never arise again. And this very absence of any aim gave him the complete, joyous sense of freedom that constituted his happiness at this time.

He could not see an aim, for he now had faith—not faith in any kind of rule, or words, or ideas, but faith in an ever-living, ever-present God. Before, he had sought God through the aims he set himself. That search for an aim had been simply a search for God. And suddenly, in captivity, he had learned—not through words or reasoning but through direct feeling—what his old nurse had told him long ago: that God is here and everywhere. In captivity he had learned that in Karataev, God was greater, more infinite and unfathomable, than in the Architect of the Universe recognized by the Freemasons. He felt like a man who, after straining his eyes to see into the far distance, discovers what he sought right at his feet. All his life he had looked over the heads of the people around him, when he should have simply looked straight ahead without straining his eyes.

In the past he had never been able to find that great, inscrutable, infinite something. He had only felt that it must exist somewhere and had searched for it. In everything near and understandable, he had seen only what was limited, petty, ordinary, and meaningless. He had equipped himself with a mental telescope and peered into the distance, where the petty everyday world, hidden in mist, had seemed great and infinite simply because it wasn't clearly visible. European life, politics, Freemasonry, philosophy, philanthropy—all had seemed that way. But even then, in moments of what he had considered weakness, his mind had penetrated those distances and seen the same pettiness, worldliness, and meaninglessness there too. Now, however, he had learned to see the great, the eternal, and the infinite in everything, and so—to see it and take joy in contemplating it—he naturally threw away the telescope through which he had been gazing over people's heads, and gladly beheld the ever-changing, eternally great, unfathomable, and infinite life around him. And the closer he looked, the more at peace and happy he became. That terrible question "What for?"—which had once demolished all his mental constructions—no longer existed for him. To that question, "What for?" a simple answer now always stood ready in his soul: "Because there is a God, that God without whose will not a single hair falls from a man's head."
